item.title: Crostesting makes no sense?
item.content:encoded:
Ok, I need a really good explanation. This object needs a specific pose to work.

(achieved by having the arm with the bracelets completely extended in front of oneself, with the opposing arm extended up to the elbow of the fully extended arm)

but

SCP-1884-A has no hands; instead, its forearms are joined together where the wrist joints are typically located.

Joined together. That would mean… no way to wear the bracelets, or make the bow pose.
Also, no multiple arms, just two. Unless the idea is that she shoots arms from SCP-1884-B, which is never explained either? And… would also make no sense since -B's is hands from the wrist, no arms/forearms to shoot?

I personally joined back when cross-testing was frowned upon, so seeing this wiki-walk things was weird now that I re-joined… I -really- am trying to ignore them… but this one makes zero sense to me.

item.title: Why is this 'Euclid'?
item.content:encoded:
While I might be relatively new, it seems to me as if this object fulfills all the requirements for being safe.

- it displays no sentience whatsoever.
- it's properties are fully understood and well-documented.
- it's properties only manifest in a specific, easily controlled circumstance
- no containment procedures beyond 'locked box' are necessary.

item.title: Staff Post - Open
item.content:encoded:
Edits made. Timer Removed. See Below for Details.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 72 hours if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

So in reading this article, my initial thought was what happens if an individual with multiple arms/hands attempts to use these bracelets? Can they rapid fire multiple limbs like a kind of twisted Hawkeye or Legolas? Turns out we have an article in which a humanoid has access to multiple hands in SCP-1884. As such, I think it would be interesting to propose the following addition:

Editing the following section:

When the "bowstring is pulled and released", the bones of the arm will be forcibly ejected from the extended limb, traveling in a straight path at speeds recorded over three hundred (300) meters per second. The missing bones and resulting damage to the arm are quickly regenerated, and the weapon is capable of being "fired" again within minutes.

To this:

When the "bowstring is pulled and released", the bones of the arm will be forcibly ejected from the extended limb, traveling in a straight path at speeds recorded over three hundred (300) meters per second. The missing bones and resulting damage to the arm are quickly regenerated, and the weapon is capable of being "fired" again within minutes. Tests using subjects possessing multiple arms/hands, such as SCP-1884-A, have demonstrated the ability to fire SCP-154 several times, with the bones of different arms being used with each successive firing.

This addition conveys the imagery of SCP-1884-A firing this several times, using SCP-1884-B as a kind of repeating bow before testing stopped, likely due to SCP-1884-B interference.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
"Most often this manifests simply as minor mutations of the original subject, such as changes in size, pigmentation, and structure of the original organelles."

Am I the only one who finds the sudden leap from discussion of bones and gross anatomical structure to cellular structure, then back again with no fanfare, disorienting? Maybe the author meant to use a term other than organelles?

Assuming the terminology is correct, rewording it to "Most often this manifests simply as minor mutations of the original subject, such as changes in size, pigmentation, and structure of affected tissue on a cellular level" makes it less jarring.

If he meant the bones and surrounding tissues themselves are affected on a visible, macro level, then rewording it to "Most often this manifests simply as minor mutations of the original subject, such as changes in size, pigmentation, and structure of the regenerated tissue" is a better way of saying it.

Or am I the only one who ever noticed/cared?
